body:
SUPERSEDES THIS TICKET'S OWN FIRST DRAFT, same id. Myk settled the model in chat on 2026-07-28,
walking it at the object level (Alice/Bob/Charlie). The first draft feared "a granted connector becomes
a lawful striker at root". That fear is structurally moot under the settled model: a connection never
acts at root, so the striker-set question never arises. This body records the model as ruled, the code
facts verified against it, and the questions P1 still owes.

THE SETTLED MODEL (Myk, 2026-07-28):

1. A CONNECTION BINDS TO EXACTLY ONE CONTAINER. That binding is its whole world: reads gather that
   container — everything in it, wherever it originated — and writes land in it. The binding is an
   UPPER BOUND, not a routing rule: a connection bound wide (Bob's, at his user root) addresses
   sub-containers through query semantics; a connection bound narrow (Alice's `alice.folklore`) simply
   cannot reach outside. Same mechanism, different owner choice.
2. THE OWNER ACTS, THE CONNECTION CARRIES. Every read and write through the connection is made by the
   container's owner in their capacity AS owner. The operator never appears on this path — it is an
   administrative capacity of the store, orthogonal to ownership. (Not precluded: the store's top level
   is just a container, so a connection COULD bind to it. A guard, if wanted, is a later ticket.)
3. ATTRIBUTION IS PER-CONNECTION, AUTHORITY IS THE OWNER'S. Myk chose option (b), in his words:
   "It's Alice (via MCP connection scoped to the folklore container with id xyz)." Each connection gets
   its own signing key, provably the owner's — granted by her, resolving to her. Deltas read as Alice
   everywhere; forensics can still say WHICH connection wrote what; a leaked connector credential has a
   one-connection blast radius. Keys buy provenance, never privilege (plan §9a), applied one level down.
4. A NEGATION IS AN ORDINARY DELTA, AND MEMBERSHIP DECIDES ITS REACH (Myk, verbatim ruling): "If both
   D1 and D2 are in the gathered deltas for some HyperView, then the Schema resolver for views over
   that hyperview should know that D2 negates D1" — and "it doesn't matter who wrote the negation."
   The Schema decides what in-play means (hide, mark retracted, whatever the Policy says). So trust
   moves from READ TIME to ADMISSION TIME: writing into a container, or accepting into it via
   federation, is the deliberate act; once in, in play. Per-container divergence falls out of
   membership alone — D1 in two containers, D2 admitted to one: negated there, preserved in the other.
   This is also the version-update story for public aggregators: you admit the publisher's negation,
   and it binds because you admitted it.

CODE FACTS, VERIFIED 2026-07-28 (not assumed):

- `containerScope` (src/gateway/container.ts, membersOf) ALREADY implements the read half: a shared
  container's members are whatever its MEMBERSHIP TERM selects from the primary ground; a separate
  container's members are its own pool's snapshot, wholesale. It returns the operand set and readers
  resolve over it — so "in the gathered set = in play" is the substrate's existing behaviour. The H9
  refusals (unattached pool, unresolvable membership address, no membership) are already in place.
- A container declaration carries `membership` inline OR by published address (`membershipAt`), and
  trust/posture are immutable per container, enforced at the door.
- Grants today target STORE_ENTITY at CTX_GRANTS (src/gateway/accounts.ts, grantShaped). Binding a
  grant to a CONTAINER entity instead is the generalisation this ticket designs — the consent page then
  names the container, and the grant cannot exceed it, which retires the "consent copy understates the
  power" problem structurally rather than by disclosure.
- `lawfulStrikersJson` remains the ROOT/governed-read mechanism and this ticket DOES NOT TOUCH IT.
  The first draft's finding (adminsOnly=false ignores the verb at accounts.ts:148/:167) stays true and
  stays out of scope here: connections never enter that path.

WHERE H1 RELOCATES, and it is the heart of the rails: the bug class is no longer "whose strike counts"
but A GATHER THAT INCLUDES D1 AND DROPS A D2 THAT IS A MEMBER. A separate container gets closure
physically (everything in the pool is in the set). A SHARED container's membership Term must be written
so that admitting a claim admits its negations — a Term shaped to select claims-only strands every
admitted strike. P1 must state the discipline (does the Term author owe it, or does the gather close
over negations mechanically?) and the rail asserts BOTH LEVELS: D2 is in the membership (delta level)
AND the view resolves without D1 (object level). Two-sided everywhere: the folklore read hides D1, the
friends read still shows it, and a named live bystander in folklore survives.

THE OPEN P1 QUESTIONS:

(a) NESTING: when a query runs at the parent, does it gather a child container's members automatically,
    or is membership explicit per container with children ADDRESSABLE but not auto-merged? Lean:
    membership is explicit; nesting is addressing, not gather semantics; composition is a read-time
    choice. Verify what membership Terms already do before deciding.
(b) THE KEY'S SHAPE: what delta says "this key is Alice's, for connection xyz, bound to container C"?
    It must be readable at the door (which container may this key write?) and at forensics time (which
    connection wrote this?). Likely a grant whose subject is the connection key and whose target entity
    is the container — P1 designs the exact claims and their admission rule.
(c) REVOCATION: striking the connection grant kills the transport and the key's write standing. Past
    deltas keep their author. Two-sided rail: revoked connection's write refuses; a SECOND connection's
    write still lands.
(d) WRITE ENFORCEMENT: the door must refuse a connection-signed write whose target falls outside the
    bound container. Where does that check live, and what exactly is "outside" for a shared container
    whose membership is a Term? (A write cannot be pre-tested against a Term that selects by content —
    P1 must resolve how a write is FILED INTO a container at the append door.)

DEFERRED, deliberately: operator promotion of container claims (reuse T33's promote-LAW when something
needs it); any guard on binding a connection to the store's top level; the adminsOnly verb-check gap at
root (its own finding, its own ticket if Myk wants it).

RAILS: none declared here, per plan §9e — declared at P3 when the tests exist and are red.

DESIGN-STAGE: it decides what the system promises. Working spec at .adlc/specs/39-connection-container.md,
every criterion naming its verification, then STOP for Myk. The landing PR is his merge.

edges.contract: Phase 14 is the consent page. Under the settled model the page NAMES THE CONTAINER the connection binds to, and the grant cannot exceed it — honesty by construction instead of by disclosure. T138 defines the binding and the grant shape the page describes, so its design must precede the page's copy and the page's rails.

Phase 15 files the connector grant and mints the per-connection key. T138 decides what that grant SAYS — subject = the connection's key, target = the bound container, authority = the owner. Landing T138's design first means the grant is born container-bound, and no store ever holds an unscoped connector grant that a later change would have to narrow (a promise change owing a §20 step).

title: An MCP connection binds to a container — reads gather it, writes land in it as the owner, signed by a per-connection key
